title: The Axioms of Probability
short: Every probability rule follows from three: P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, and the probabilities of disjoint events add.
trouble: Students accept an assignment of probabilities that adds to more than 1, or add P(A) + P(B) for events that overlap.

blocks.html: In the addition rule you met rules such as $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$ and $P(A^{c}) = 1 - P(A)$. They feel like separate facts, but each one follows from three short statements. Probability as a branch of mathematics starts from these three axioms, set down by Andrey Kolmogorov in 1933, and every rule in this course is built on them.

A sample space $S$ is the set of all outcomes of an experiment, and an event is a set of outcomes (a subset of $S$). We write $A^{c}$ for the complement of $A$ (some books write $A'$), and call events disjoint (or mutually exclusive) when they share no outcome.

Every familiar rule is a short consequence.
Complement: $A$ and $A^{c}$ are disjoint and together make $S$, so axioms 3 and 2 give $P(A) + P(A^{c}) = 1$. With $A = S$ this also shows $P(\varnothing) = 0$.
Bigger events are more likely: if $A \subseteq B$, then $B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \cap A^{c}$, so $P(B) = P(A) + P(B \cap A^{c}) \ge P(A)$. In particular $P(A) \le P(S) = 1$.
Addition rule: $A \cup B$ is the disjoint union of $A$ and $B \cap A^{c}$, while $B$ is the disjoint union of $A \cap B$ and $B \cap A^{c}$. Subtracting, $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$

blocks.name: prob-square
blocks.cap: The sample space as a unit square: each event is a region and its probability is its area. Drag the edges and watch the readout keep every rule true.

blocks.html: The square is a good mental model: area is never negative (axiom 1), the whole square has area 1 (axiom 2), and areas of regions that do not overlap add (axiom 3). It also makes two bounds easy to see. An overlap fits inside each event, so $P(A \cap B) \le \min(P(A), P(B))$. And a union is never bigger than the whole square or than the two areas together, so $P(A \cup B) \le \min(1,\ P(A) + P(B))$.

blocks.title: Finding a missing probability
blocks.q: A spinner lands on red, blue, green or yellow. $P(\text{red}) = 0.15$, $P(\text{blue}) = 0.3$ and $P(\text{green}) = 0.25$. Find $P(\text{yellow})$.
steps: The four outcomes are disjoint and together they make up $S$.
By axioms 3 and 2, their probabilities add to 1.

blocks.title: How much must two events overlap?
blocks.q: $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.6$. What is the smallest possible value of $P(A \cap B)$?
steps: By the addition rule, $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$$
$P(A \cup B)$ is at most 1, so $P(A \cap B) \ge 0.7 + 0.6 - 1 = 0.3$.
The value $0.3$ is reached when $A \cup B$ is the whole sample space.
blocks.a: $0.3$: the events must overlap at least that much.

blocks.title: Spotting an impossible claim
blocks.q: Someone reports $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.45$. Is this possible?
blocks.a: No: an overlap can never be more likely than either event.

blocks.html: Two common slips. First, a list of probabilities for outcomes that cannot happen together must add to exactly 1; a list adding to $1.1$ is not a probability model. Second, adding $P(A) + P(B)$ for events that overlap: if each of Saturday and Sunday has a $0.6$ chance of rain, the chance of rain on the weekend is not $1.2$. Check: any answer above 1 is wrong, and the addition rule needs the overlap subtracted.
